title: Bar Avin (or Bar Ova)
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: He was a distinguished preacher already in Rava’s time. In Moed Katan 25b, when Rava came to the Tigris (Rashi in Ein Yaakov explains: when he was crossing the river; another explanation is that the Tigris was in flood and threatened to sweep things away), he told Bar Avin, “Rise and say something.” He rose and said, “The greater part of ‘the third’ has come into the waters; remember and have mercy. We have strayed from following You like a woman from her husband; do not abandon us like the sign of the bitter water.” Hyman says he lived a long life, so that even in Rav Ashi’s time he and his colleague Bar Kipok were eulogists, as it is said there: Rav Ashi asked Bar Kipok, “On that day (when Ravina died, according to Rabbenu Chananel), what did you say?” He said to him, “I said: If a flame has fallen among the cedars—”. Bar Avin said to him, “Heaven forbid!” “And what did you say?” “I said: Weep for the mourners—”. Rav Ashi was offended by them, and their feet became twisted. On that day (when Rav Ashi died, though Hyman says it appears more likely to refer to Ravina) they did not come to eulogize him. This is what Rav Ashi said: “Neither Bar Kipok performs chalitzah nor Bar Avin.” (Sefer HaYuchasin reads Bar Ova and Bar Kippuz.)

notes.text: Hyman’s river interpretation comes through Rashi in Ein Yaakov; the supplied spelling does not mean a date palm here. The prayer’s “third” is compressed and remains a source question. “Bitter water” evokes the ordeal of a suspected unfaithful wife, not an unrelated geographical place.

Rashi on Moed Katan25b explains the concluding chalitzah remark through the twisted feet and the legal requirement of removing the shoe from the foot. Hyman’s competing Rav Ashi/Ravina death references are preserved rather than chronologically harmonized.

Two whole saved digital scalars were read, with raw SHA256, exact selectors, scalar hashes and actual edition metadata checked: William Davidson Moed Katan25b, versions[0].text[6] (231 characters), and Vilna Edition Rashi on Moed Katan25b, versions[0].text[6][1] (94 characters). The Rashi gloss says Israel are called the third and Rava is equal to the majority of Israel; this is an attributed commentary explanation, not wording inserted into Hyman's prayer. The body retains the compressed majority of the third, the plural we have strayed, remember and have mercy, the wife/husband comparison and the sign of the bitter water. The saved Gemara has לדגלת and Rashi's selected gloss concerns only the third. Neither selected scalar contains Hyman's Ein Yaakov river explanations, the later eulogy exchange, Rabbenu Chananel's death reference or the concluding chalitzah commentary. Thus the existing river and chalitzah notes remain historical editorial claims, not newly verified whole-passage findings. Hyman's supplied הדקל and חדקל remain unchanged; a Tigris interpretation does not prove a scribal error or printing history. בע"י is contextually read as Ein Yaakov and ר"ח as Rabbenu Chananel; the latter is not an expansion of Rashi's name. Hyman's claim that Bar Avin lived long into Rav Ashi's time and his more-likely Ravina death reference remain attributed claims, without a new chronological or identity admission. The two questions and first-person proposed eulogy answers remain explicit; the conditional rhetorical setting is not independently settled by the selected prayer scalar. Full Rav is preserved at every explicit Ashi occurrence; Rava and Ravina remain untitled proper names. Bar Avin, Bar Ova, Bar Kipok and Bar Kippuz retain their different spellings without identity harmonization or new genealogy. The interrupted eulogies keep their dashes, Heaven forbid, the offended reaction, twisted feet and both negated chalitzah clauses. The current two mixed notes and the original uncertainty note remain exact in their versions; no note retirement or source-question resolution is applied. Hold p001 remains. No extra poem, legal requirements, narrative continuation or verses from the primary texts are imported, and no printed pixels or correction history were verified.

The printed notice spans volume I, pp. 283–284. It reads חדקל for the river beside the supplied הדקל; no Hebrew change is made. The consulted Rashi on Moed Katan 25b identifies the river as the Tigris and explains “the third” as Israel, with Rava equal to its majority. This is an attributed explanation of the compressed prayer, not an extra clause inserted into it. The full consulted Gemara gives the eulogies, the offense, the twisted feet and both negated chalitzah clauses. Rashi explicitly relates chalitzah to the position of their feet; his gloss on “that day” does not itself name the deceased. Rabbeinu Chananel explicitly names Ravina and describes an intended future eulogy. Hyman’s “what did you say?” and “I said,” his Rav Ashi/Ravina alternatives, and his preference for Ravina are retained and distinguished from that presentation. His conclusion that Bar Avin lived from Rava’s time into Rav Ashi’s remains his chronological reconstruction. The omitted parts of the poems are not inserted after Hyman’s dashes. His exact Ein Yaakov and Yuchasin editions have not been independently collated; Bar Avin/Bar Ova and Bar Kipok/Bar Kippuz do not become new identity bindings. The earlier notes retain their historical inspection limits.
